title: Mean
body:
Add everything up, divide by how many there are. The **arithmetic mean** is the balance point of
the data: the value about which the deviations cancel.

$$
\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i
\qquad\text{(sample)}
\qquad\qquad
\mu = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i
\qquad\text{(population)}
$$

The formula is identical; the symbol is not. $\bar{x}$ is a **statistic**, computed from data you
have. $\mu$ is a **parameter**, a property of a population you almost never see. Half of
[[STATISTICS]] is the question of how close the first gets to the second, and the answer is
[[Sampling Distribution]] and the [[Central Limit Theorem]].

## The balance-point property

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i - \bar{x}) = 0
$$

Always, exactly, for every dataset. The mean is the unique point where the deviations above and
below cancel, which is why it is the centre of mass of the data and why every deviation-based
formula in the course measures from it. It is also the reason [[Variance]] has to square the
deviations before summing: the unsquared sum is zero and carries no information.

Slightly stronger, and it is the link out to the rest of the vault: **$\bar{x}$ is the value $c$
that minimises $\sum(x_i - c)^2$.** Differentiate and set to zero and $c = \bar{x}$ falls out. The
mean is a least squares fit with no predictors, which is exactly why [[Linear Regression]]'s line
passes through $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$ and why [[Least Squares]] in MATH 2303 is the same idea one
dimension up. Swap the squared deviations for absolute ones and the minimiser becomes the
[[Median]] instead.

## The weakness

The mean uses every value, which makes it efficient and makes it fragile. One bad observation
moves it without limit:

```
data:       2  3  3  4  4  5  5  6        mean 4.0    median 4
data:       2  3  3  4  4  5  5  600      mean 78.3   median 4
```

The [[Median]] did not move at all. This is the entire argument for reporting a median on skewed
data, and it is why "average salary" is a much friendlier number for an employer to quote than
"median salary".

**Weighted mean** handles the case where observations do not count equally:

$$
\bar{x}_w = \frac{\sum w_i x_i}{\sum w_i}
$$

which is the same formula the discrete expected value uses with the weights being probabilities.
See [[Random Variable]].

## Where it goes next

- Every later formula that says "deviation" means deviation from $\bar{x}$: [[Variance]],
  [[Correlation]], the residuals in [[Linear Regression]], the sums of squares in [[ANOVA]].
- $\bar{X}$ is itself a [[Random Variable]] once you accept the sample was random, and the
  [[Central Limit Theorem]] says its distribution is normal with standard deviation
  $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$ no matter what the population looks like. That single fact is why the mean and
  not the median is the quantity the inference half of the course is built around.
- [[Confidence Interval]] and [[Hypothesis Testing]] are almost always statements about $\mu$.

## Related

- [[Average Value]]: the index, and the comparison against the other two measures
- [[Median]] and [[Mode]]: the robust alternatives
- [[Descriptive Statistics]]: sample versus population notation in full
- [[Principal Component Analysis]] (MATH 2303): centring a data matrix is subtracting the column
  means, and PCA is wrong without it
